Flares are also hard to manage because normal pregnancy symptoms — fatigue, fluid build-up in the joints, skin changes, hair loss, shortness of breath, and joint pain — can mimic lupus symptoms, making it difficult to distinguish a flare from a normal pregnancy.
Some lupus medications (such as methotrexate, mycophenolate, or cyclophosphamide) are harmful to the baby; some can cross the placenta and pose a threat to it.
Women often need to stop certain medications months before conceiving, and doctors may need to make important medication changes to ensure a safe pregnancy.
These antibodies (antiphospholipid antibodies) also increase the risk of miscarriage, though blood thiners can help prevent this in many women.

Women with lupus face higher risks of:
- high blood pressure (hypertension)
- pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure plus protein in the urine), which occurs in one in five women with lupus and, if left untreated, can endanger the life of both the woman and the baby
- premature labour and preterm birth
- the baby being born with low birth weight
- blood clots in the legs or lungs
- miscarriage
- emerg
